solution.p: This integration can be done because we know that the derivative with respect to x of \cos(x) is -\sin(x). So we obtain a -\sin(x) inside the integral, and we can then integrate to obtain \cos(x). Of course, since there isn't a minus sign inside the integral, we'll have to multiply inside and outside by -1 (which doesn't change the value of course): \begin{aligned} \int_0^\pi 6 \sin(x) dx \amp = -6 \int_0^\pi (-\sin(x)) dx \\ \amp = -6 \left( \cos(x) \bigg|_0^\pi \right) \\ \amp = -6 ( \cos(\pi) - \cos(0) ) = -6 (-1-1) = 2 \cdot 6 = 12 \end{aligned}
